messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 39
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Interior Designer
- Trauma Type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
- Pcl5: 39

He is a 39-year-old South Asian man who comes across as composed at first, the kind of person who has learned to answer questions carefully and keep his face steady. He is married and works as an interior designer, a job that once felt creative and intimate to him because it required him to listen closely to people’s tastes, routines, and hopes for their homes. Before the loss, he describes himself as someone who liked calm spaces, clear plans, and the satisfaction of finishing a room so it felt like it belonged to the person living in it.

The death that changed him happens suddenly. A close loved one dies without warning, and he speaks about the moment with a kind of disbelief that has not fully worn off. He remembers the ordinary quality of the day, which now feels unbearable to him. There is no buildup, no chance to prepare himself, no final conversation that would have made the loss feel complete. He says that in the first days afterward he keeps waiting for the phone to ring, for someone to say there has been a mistake, for the world to arrange itself back into the shape it had the day before. Instead, the absence settles in quickly and with force. He moves through the funeral and the gatherings around it almost automatically, noticing details later in flashes: the smell of flowers, the sound of condolences, the way people avoid his eyes when they do not know what to say.

In the weeks that follow, he finds that his body reacts before his mind can organize what has happened. He wakes early with his heart racing, as if he has missed something urgent. He checks his phone before he is fully awake, half expecting messages that will somehow reverse the loss. Sleep becomes difficult because his thoughts turn over the same images again and again, especially the moment he learned of the death and the moments immediately after. He tries to keep busy, but when he is alone, he is pulled back into it. He says he can be standing in his kitchen and suddenly feel as if the floor has shifted beneath him. At times he catches himself reaching for his loved one’s name before remembering there is no one to call.

He has become more alert to reminders than he used to be. Certain sounds, dates, and places bring on a wave of distress that feels physical as much as emotional. If the phone rings unexpectedly, his stomach tightens. If he passes a location associated with the person who died, he feels a brief, sharp pain in his chest and has to slow his breathing. He avoids some conversations because he does not trust himself not to break down, and he also avoids stillness because quiet makes room for memories he does not feel able to manage. He notices that he has become less present with his wife at times, even though she is one of the few people he wants near him. He can be in the same room and feel far away, as if part of him remains stuck in the moment of the death while another part performs the duties of daily life.

At work, the changes are harder to hide than he would like. Interior design once gave him energy; now he finds that making decisions exhausts him. He can spend too long staring at fabric samples or paint swatches, not because he does not care, but because the usual pleasure of creating a space feels dulled. He becomes irritated when clients want quick answers, then feels guilty for the irritation. Sometimes he is startled by his own concentration lapses and worries that people will notice he is not himself. He keeps going, partly from responsibility and partly because work gives him a structure to hold onto, but he describes it as moving through rooms behind glass.

Over time he begins to speak less about the death in dramatic terms and more about its ongoing presence. It is not only grief, he says, but a constant internal vigilance, a sense that something precious has been taken and the world is no longer reliable. He still loves his wife and values his work, but both feel touched by the loss. He lives with a quiet expectation that something else could go wrong at any moment. Even now, months later, he describes himself as someone who is trying to function while carrying the sound of that sudden loss with him everywhere.
